title: Following someone else's focus is described as the earlier joint-attention skill
summary: Bradley, Smith, and Wilson say responding to another person's gaze or gesture develops before the child starts directing that person's attention.
body: In their 2023 scoping review, responding to joint attention is the receptive form: the infant follows someone else's gaze or gestures and shares attention on an object. Initiating is the infant's own attention-directing behavior toward a partner. The review says responding comes first. It also says that around 8 to 9 months infants get better at following a caregiver and at starting new episodes. Those are the review's statements about the literature, not a new household survey, and not a screen.

sources.title: Qualitative and quantitative measures of joint attention development in the first year of life
sources.author: Holly Bradley, Beth A. Smith, and Rujuta B. Wilson
sources.note: Supports the claim that responding to joint attention develops before initiating it, and the note about greater skill around 8 to 9 months. Peer-reviewed open copy.

said_by: Holly Bradley, Beth Smith, and Rujuta Wilson
